'''George Claude Pimentel''' (May 2, 1922 – June 18, 1989) was a preeminent chemist and researcher, the inventor of the [[chemical laser]], who was also dedicated to science education and public service.<ref name="Moore">{{cite journal | last=Moore | first=C. Bradley | title=George Pimentel | journal=Physics Today | volume=43 | issue=3 | year=1990 | issn=0031-9228 | doi=10.1063/1.2810504 | pages=96| bibcode=1990PhT....43c..96M | doi-access= }}</ref> He developed the technique of [[matrix isolation]] in low-temperature chemistry. He also developed [[Time-resolved spectroscopy#Time-resolved_infrared_spectroscopy|time-resolved infrared spectroscopy]] to study radicals and other transient species. In the late 1960s, Pimentel led the University of California team that designed the [[Infrared spectroscopy|infrared spectrometer]] for the [[Mariner 6 and 7|Mars Mariner 6 and 7]] missions that analyzed the surface and atmosphere of [[Mars]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sigmaxi.org/programs/prizes-awards/william-procter/award-winner/george-c.-pimentel|title=George C. Pimentel|website=www.sigmaxi.org|access-date=2016-10-09}}</ref>

He was a passionate and popular teacher of first-year chemistry for his entire career. 
In science education, he was best known for the [https://archive.org/details/chemstudystory00merr/page/n7/mode/2up CHEM STUDY project], a national effort to improve high-school chemistry teaching. He participated in the production of films and other supplementary materials and in the training of teachers nationwide. Later, in 1985, he organized and edited the National Academy of Sciences' "Pimentel Report," formally known as [https://nap.nationalacademies.org/catalog/606/opportunities-in-chemistry Opportunities in Chemistry], which highlighted the most important challenges in chemistry at that time. It was a resource for general public including lawmakers. A revised version, [https://nap.nationalacademies.org/catalog/1884/opportunities-in-chemistry-today-and-tomorrow Opportunities in Chemistry Today and Tomorrow], was used worldwide for high school and college students.

An alumnus of [[University of California, Los Angeles]] (B.S. 1943) and [[University of California, Berkeley]] (Ph.D. 1949), Pimentel began teaching at Berkeley in 1949, where he remained until his death in 1989 from [[intestinal cancer]], with a three year appointment as Deputy Director at the [[National Science Foundation]] under the [[Carter administration]] in Washington, D.C..<ref name="urlGeorgeC.Pimentel">{{cite journal |url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s00897990342a.pdf |title=George C. Pimentel (1922?1989): A Retrospective Personal and Pictorial Tribute a Decade after His Death |journal=The Chemical Educator |date=December 1999 |volume=4 |issue=6 |pages=242–258 |doi=10.1007/s00897990342a |s2cid=93524208 |access-date=2020-01-31|last1=Kauffman |first1=George B. }}</ref><ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1989/06/21/obituaries/george-c-pimentel-chemist-who-led-mars-study-was-67.html New York Times Obituary: George C. Pimentel; Chemist Who Led Mars Study Was 67]</ref>

== Chemical laser ==
In 1961, [[John C. Polanyi]] was the first to point out the possibility of chemical pumping based on vibrational excitation. He proposed four possible reactions, one of which was the reaction of H + Cl<sub>2</sub>. Using an infrared spectrometer, Jerome Kasper and Pimentel discovered infrared pulses produced by photodissociation of iodine, the first chemical laser. In September 1964, they announced their discovery at the first conference on chemical lasers, by that time more than 100 possible chemical reactions and 60 photodissociation reactions were proposed capable of producing laser radiation. However, at the symposium in [[San Diego]] only one working laser was reported, which was laced with photodissociation of iodine. 

In 1965, Kasper and Pimentel discovered the laser radiation HCl, arising from the explosion of the system H<sub>2</sub> / Cl<sub>2</sub>. After the discovery of the laser based on the reaction of F + H<sub>2</sub> in 1967, the number of chemical lasers found by the Pimentel laboratory rapidly increased. Thus, Pimentel first transformed the chemical energy obtained as a result of vibrational excitation into laser radiation.

==Honors and awards==
In 1966, Pimentel was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] and in 1968 to the American Academy of Arts and Science. In 1987 and 1989 he was elected an honorary member of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry|Royal Chemical Society]] (Great Britain), and the Royal Institute of Great Britain.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.worldofchemicals.com/255/chemistry-articles/george-claude-pimentel-inventor-of-chemical-laser.html|title=George Claude Pimentel – inventor of chemical laser|date=2013-04-30|access-date=2018-07-13|archive-date=2018-07-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180714021739/http://www.worldofchemicals.com/255/chemistry-articles/george-claude-pimentel-inventor-of-chemical-laser.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1987, he served as the [[President of the American Chemical Society]].

The ACS Award in Chemical Education was renamed the [[George C. Pimentel Award in Chemical Education]] in his honor in 1989.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://georgecpimentel.tripod.com/gcp-award.htm|title=Awards Named for George C. Pimentel|website=georgecpimentel.tripod.com|access-date=2016-10-09|archive-date=2004-05-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040527104011/http://georgecpimentel.tripod.com/gcp-award.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/george-c-pimentel-award-in-chemical-education.html|title=George C. Pimentel Award in Chemical Education - American Chemical Society|website=American Chemical Society|access-date=2016-10-09}}</ref>
